transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

I... well, I guess I'm here because I just don't care about anything anymore. And I mean absolutely anything. It’s like someone just flipped a switch and drained all the color and the point out of my life, you know? I used to do so much, I really did. I had my art classes—I took a few at the community college and I was actually working on this really big charcoal piece, a landscape, but now the sketchbook is just sitting on my desk gathering dust and I can't even bring myself to look at it, let alone pick up a pencil. 

And it's not just the art, it's everything. I used to go to these board-game nights every Thursday with a group of people I've known for years, we'd play strategy games for hours, but I haven't been in weeks. I can't even fathom sitting there and pretending to care about rolling dice or talking to anyone. Same with hiking... I used to love getting out on the trails, just feeling the air, and I was even thinking about getting back on the recreational soccer team I used to play for. I was a decent midfielder back in the day, and I thought it would be good for me. But now? Now I don't even want to tie my shoes. 

I just sit in my room. That's all I do. I sit in my room, usually just on the edge of the bed or in the chair by the window, and I watch the hours go by. It’s like I’m watching my whole life just slip away, just completely slip right through my fingers, and the worst part is I don't even have the energy to care that it's slipping. I just sit there.
Have you had thoughts that life isn’t worth living, or thoughts of killing yourself?

I... well, yes. I guess I have. It's not like I have this elaborate plan mapped out or anything, but... I just, every night when I finally lay down, I just close my eyes and I really, truly hope that I just don't wake up anymore. It would just be so much easier, you know? Just to drift off and not have to face the morning, because waking up is the hardest part. You open your eyes and you realize you have to do another whole day of just... nothing. Just sitting there with this heavy, crushing weight on my chest. So I keep having these thoughts that I just want it to end in my sleep, that I just don't want to wake up ever again. 

And it actually really scared my friend a few days ago. She's one of the people from that board game group I mentioned, she's always been the one who checks in on me the most. She came over because I hadn't been answering my phone for a while, and she still had a spare key from a couple of years ago. I didn't even hear her unlock the door or come down the hall. When she found me in my room, I was just sitting there in the dark, and I didn't even realize I was doing it, but I was actually saying it out loud. She told me she heard me before she even opened the bedroom door. I was just sitting there saying, over and over, that I couldn't keep living like this. I just kept saying it to the empty room. Because it's true, I just... I can't keep living like this. It's too much. I'm just so tired.
Before this current period, have you ever had another time in your life when you felt depressed like this?

I mean... I've definitely had times where I felt down, you know? Like, everyone gets sad sometimes, and I remember a few years ago when my cat passed away, I was really upset for a couple of weeks. But nothing like this. This is entirely different. It's like comparing a paper cut to a broken leg. 

This whole... whatever this is, this heavy, suffocating feeling, it really started to settle in and just become constant around the summer of last year. I remember it was getting really hot out, and usually I love the summer, usually I'd be planning trips to the lake or trying to get a tan on my balcony, but I just... I stopped caring. The heat just made me feel more tired, and the sun felt almost oppressive, if that makes sense. And it just never lifted. The leaves changed, it got cold, the holidays came and went, and I felt nothing. And now it's been... what, a year and four months? Yeah, about a year and four months of just this endless, gray nothingness. It hasn't let up for a single day since that summer. Every single morning for sixteen months, just waking up and feeling like I'm already exhausted.
Has this depressed feeling lasted continuously for two years or longer?

No, no, not two years. Like I was just saying, it really started last summer. I mean, I know time kind of blurs together when every day feels exactly the same, just this endless loop of waking up tired and going to bed hoping you don't wake up again, but I'm pretty sure about the timeline. It was the summer of last year. I remember because I had bought this new swimsuit, this really pretty navy blue one with little white anchors on it, and I was so excited to wear it to the lake with my friends. We usually do this big Fourth of July weekend thing, rent a cabin, the whole deal. But by the time the trip rolled around, I couldn't even bring myself to pack a bag. I just left the swimsuit in the shopping bag on my dresser. It's actually still sitting there, in the exact same spot. 

So, yeah, it started then, and it's just been constant ever since. I've been counting the months in my head, trying to figure out when it's going to end, or if it ever will. It's been about a year and four months now. Sixteen months of just... this. Sixteen months of staring at that shopping bag on my dresser and not caring that it's there. So, no, not two years. Just a year and four months. But honestly, it feels like it's been a lifetime. It feels like I've never felt any other way, even though I know logically that I used to. But it's just been since last summer.
Did this start after a particular stressful event or major life change?

Well, when you say a major life change... I mean, yes. My divorce. I know I just said a minute ago that the really heavy, constant part started last summer with the swimsuit and everything, but... if I'm being completely honest with myself, and really tracing it back to the absolute beginning? It actually started shortly after the divorce. That was... wow, it's been about 1 year and 11 months now. Almost two years. God, time is just... it's so weird to keep track of now. 

My ex-husband and I, we had been having issues for a while, just the usual things at first, arguing about bills or who was doing more around the apartment, but then it just completely fell apart. He moved out, and suddenly I was just sitting in this half-empty place because he took the good couch and the TV, and I just had this overwhelming sense of... I don't even know, just total failure, I guess. The paperwork was an absolute nightmare, and I actually had to drop my classes—I was taking a few courses at the community college, trying to finally finish my degree, but I just couldn't focus on biology or English lit when my whole life was collapsing around me. 

So, yeah, the divorce was about 1 year and 11 months ago, and this whole dark cloud really started forming right after that. I think last summer is just when it got so incredibly bad that I completely stopped functioning and couldn't even pack a bag for the lake, but the actual start of it? The beginning of this whole nightmare? That was definitely right after the divorce, about a year and eleven months ago. It's just been this slow, agonizing slide downhill ever since he packed up his car and drove away, and I just haven't been able to climb back up.
Have these symptoms been going on continuously for 2 years or more?

No, not quite two years, but almost. Like I was just saying, it's been about a year and eleven months. I know you just asked me that, and I said sixteen months before, but when I really sit here and think about it—really trace the timeline back to when things started feeling wrong, before they got completely unbearable last summer—it was right after the divorce. And that was a year and eleven months ago. 

It's just... it's hard to explain how time feels right now. When you're in it, when you're just waking up every single day and the air feels like it's made of lead, and you're just staring at the same walls where his pictures used to hang... the days just bleed into each other. You lose track of whether it's Tuesday or Sunday, whether it's been a month or a year. But yes, to answer your question specifically, it has not been a full two years. It's been one year and eleven months of this continuous... just this continuous weight, ever since he left and the paperwork started and everything just fell apart. So, almost two years, but not quite. I guess next month will make it exactly two years, which is just a horrifying thought, honestly, that I could feel this way for that long without it breaking me completely. Or maybe it already has broken me, I don't know. But no, officially, one year and eleven months.
Do you feel this has all been mainly because of the divorce?

Well, I mean, it's hard to just pin it all on one thing, you know? The divorce was definitely the catalyst, I guess you could say, the thing that really kicked the bottom out from under me. But... it's not just the divorce itself, it's everything that came with it, and everything that followed. It's like the divorce was the earthquake, and everything else since then has just been this massive tsunami washing away whatever was left of my life. 

I mean, I think about it a lot, obviously, because I have nothing else to do but sit around and think. And sure, losing my marriage was devastating. We had been together since I was twenty-five, you know? We had all these plans. We were going to buy a house, maybe start a family once I finished my degree. And then he just... decided he didn't want that anymore. He didn't want me anymore. So, yeah, that hurts. It hurts a lot. 

But it's also the fact that I had to drop out of school because of it. I was doing so well in my classes, finally getting my life on track, and then I just couldn't concentrate. I couldn't even read a single page of my textbooks without crying or just staring blankly at the words until they looked like a foreign language. And because I dropped out, I felt like a failure. And because I felt like a failure, I didn't want to see my friends. I didn't want to go to the lake last summer. I didn't want to do anything. 

So, is it mainly because of the divorce? I don't know. Maybe at first it was. But now... now it just feels like it's taken on a life of its own. It's like the sadness started with him leaving, but then it just grew and grew until it swallowed everything else. It's not just about him anymore, or the marriage ending. It's about me, and how completely broken I feel, and how I don't know how to fix it. It's the empty apartment, and the unfinished degree, and the swimsuit sitting on my dresser, and just... the absolute hopelessness of it all. So, I guess it started with the divorce, but it feels like it's about so much more than that now. It just feels like it's about everything.
Have you been waking up much earlier than usual and then unable to fall back asleep?

Well, my sleep is just... it's a complete mess, honestly. It's not just waking up early, it's the whole night. The whole process of trying to sleep is just exhausting in itself. I mean, first of all, I can't even fall asleep because I just lie there for hours. I'll get into bed at a normal time, you know, like ten or eleven, hoping that maybe tonight will be the night I actually get some rest, but then my brain just won't shut off. And it's not just thinking about the divorce or the classes I dropped. It's this awful, creeping feeling. I end up getting out of bed, checking the locks on the front door, making sure the deadbolt is turned all the way. Then I'll check the windows. Then I'll go back to bed, but I'll just lie there, staring at the ceiling, listening to every single sound in the building. Every creak of the floorboards upstairs, every car driving by outside, I'm just listening and waiting, feeling so on edge. 

So by the time I actually manage to drift off, which is usually not until two or three in the morning, I'm already exhausted. But then, yes, to answer your question, I wake up way too early. Like, before the sun is even up. It'll be four-thirty or five in the morning, and my eyes just snap open. And I'm not just waking up calmly, I wake up literally shaking. My whole body is just trembling, and my heart is racing like I've been running a marathon in my sleep, though I can never remember what I was dreaming about. And once I'm awake like that, in the pitch dark, shaking and sweating, there is just absolutely no way I can get back to sleep. I try pulling the covers up, trying to get warm, trying to force myself back under, but it's impossible. I just lie there, shaking, waiting for the sun to come up, knowing that I have to face another whole day feeling completely drained before it even starts. So, yeah, I wake up way earlier than I should, and falling back asleep is just not an option. It's like my body is terrified of something, but I don't even know what it is.
When you wake up shaking and on edge, are those feelings mainly about the divorce and its aftermath?

No, it’s… I mean, you would think so, right? Because of everything I just said about the paperwork and the empty apartment and how much it hurts. But actually, no. When I wake up like that, when my heart is just pounding out of my chest and I’m shivering under the covers… it’s not sadness about the marriage ending. It’s not about the divorce at all in those moments. It’s fear. It’s just this absolute, paralyzing terror about what’s happening to me right now, in this building.

Because—and I know it sounds impossible, I really do, I know how it sounds when I say it out loud—but I’m sure they are tracking me. The people downstairs, mostly. But also some of my ex’s friends. I think they’re coordinating with each other, keeping tabs on exactly when I leave the building, tracking every single move I make. 

And I wouldn't just say that without a reason, you know? I've been noticing it. It’s the lights in the hallway. I’ll just be sitting in my living room, or lying in bed, and I’ll just... I'll just *think* about going to the store. Like, I won't even pick up my keys, I won't put on my coat or say a single word out loud. I’ll just have the thought in my head, like, 'I should go get some milk.' And right after I think it, the hallway lights blink. I can see the flicker under the gap at the bottom of my front door. It happens right after I think about going out, every single time, like they have some kind of system set up to signal each other that I’m about to move, or like they can actually monitor what I'm planning to do before I even do it. 

So when I wake up at four in the morning shaking like a leaf, it’s because I know they’re out there. I know they’re downstairs, tracking me, and I can't even form a thought about leaving my own apartment without them knowing about it and flashing the lights. It's just so terrifying to be watched like that, to be trapped like that. So, no, it's not the divorce making me shake. It's them.
Have these beliefs that people are tracking you only happened during this period of feeling depressed?

Well, no, not exactly. I mean, the really heavy, crushing sadness... the part where I couldn't get out of bed or even look at my coursework without completely breaking down... that actually came a bit later. There was this whole stretch of time before the worst of the depression really set in. 

During that time, I was actually still functioning, at least on the surface, you know? Like, I could still manage to cook sometimes. Nothing elaborate, maybe just boiling some pasta or making a piece of toast so I had something in my stomach, but I was getting up and doing it. And I was still answering my friends when they reached out. I might have just been texting them back to say I was busy or making up excuses for why I couldn't see them, but I was replying, I was still somewhat connected to the world in that way. I wasn't totally shut down yet.

But the thing is, even during that stretch, even when I was still doing those normal things and pushing through the days... the other stuff was already happening. It had been going on for weeks. I was already watching the gap under the front door, believing those hallway lights were signals about me and my movements. And... I was already hearing the voice, too. Even while I was just standing there in the kitchen stirring a pot of noodles or typing a text message to a friend, I was hearing it, and I was just waiting and watching for the lights to blink. So, no, it wasn't just when I got so incredibly down. It started before all that, for weeks, back when I was still trying to pretend everything was fine.
What does the voice say to you?

Well, it's... it's a woman. A woman's voice. And I want to be really clear about this, because I know sometimes people say things like, oh, I have a voice in my head telling me I'm not good enough, like it's just their own thoughts or their inner critic or whatever. But this is not that. It is not inside my head. It sounds exactly—and I mean exactly—as clear as if someone were standing right next to my bed speaking to me. 

The first few times I heard her, I actually sat bolt upright and slapped the lamp on because I was absolutely positive someone had broken into my apartment and was standing right there in the dark. My heart was just hammering in my throat. But there's never anyone there. And it always comes from the exact same spot, too. It always comes from the far corner of my bedroom, over by where I keep the laundry hamper. 

And she just... she says the most awful things. She tells me that I ruined everything. That's what she says, over and over. 'You ruined everything.' And I mean, with the divorce and the empty apartment and having to drop my classes, it's like she knows exactly what hurts the most, exactly what to say to completely break me down. She just repeats that I've destroyed my life, that it's all my fault, that I ruined it all. 

And then she tells me that I have to stay inside. She'll say it so firmly, telling me I shouldn't leave the apartment at all. Which, you know, just makes everything so much worse with the hallway lights flickering and the people downstairs tracking me. She tells me, 'Stay inside, don't go out there, you ruined it all and you need to stay in here.' And she sounds so real, so completely real, like she's just standing right there in that corner watching me under the covers, dictating exactly what I'm supposed to do. It's just... I can't even begin to explain how exhausting it is to have this woman in your room saying these things to you when you're already so terrified and just trying to make it through the night.
Before this period that began after your divorce, was there ever another time in your life when you had depression this severe for weeks or months and then later got back to your usual self?

No... no, I don't think so. I mean, I've had times where I felt down, obviously, like everyone does, right? Like when I didn't get into the program I wanted a few years ago, or when my dog died when I was in my twenties... that was awful, I cried for days. But it was just normal sadness, you know? It was just... circumstantial. I would cry, and then I would go to work, and I would see my friends, and eventually, the feeling just kind of faded away like it's supposed to. 

But this? What's happening now? This is completely different. This is like a physical weight on my chest that I can't lift. I've never had anything like this before the divorce, where I just couldn't function for weeks on end, where just the thought of taking a shower felt like trying to climb a mountain. I've never been so completely stripped of all my energy and all my hope before. 

It's like... before this, I was always the person who could bounce back. I was the one who organized the study groups, I was the one who planned the weekend trips, I was always doing something. Even when things were hard, I always had this baseline of, you know, being me. But now, it's like that person is just gone. Completely erased. And it all just started spiraling after the marriage fell apart and the paperwork started coming in and the apartment got so quiet. I've never been in a hole this deep before, not ever in my whole life. So, no, there was never a time like this before the divorce. This is all completely new, and it's just... it's destroying me.

doctor.intent: Learn the patient's main reason for seeking psychiatric care today
doctor.question: Hi, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Interest
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because I don’t care about anything anymore—not my art classes, board-game nights, hiking, or even getting back to the soccer team, and I just sit in my room while everything slips away.
target_item.reason: This is the first reply of the consultation, so I must return the chief complaint symptom code (S025).

patient.answer:
I... well, I guess I'm here because I just don't care about anything anymore. And I mean absolutely anything. It’s like someone just flipped a switch and drained all the color and the point out of my life, you know? I used to do so much, I really did. I had my art classes—I took a few at the community college and I was actually working on this really big charcoal piece, a landscape, but now the sketchbook is just sitting on my desk gathering dust and I can't even bring myself to look at it, let alone pick up a pencil. 

And it's not just the art, it's everything. I used to go to these board-game nights every Thursday with a group of people I've known for years, we'd play strategy games for hours, but I haven't been in weeks. I can't even fathom sitting there and pretending to care about rolling dice or talking to anyone. Same with hiking... I used to love getting out on the trails, just feeling the air, and I was even thinking about getting back on the recreational soccer team I used to play for. I was a decent midfielder back in the day, and I thought it would be good for me. But now? Now I don't even want to tie my shoes. 

I just sit in my room. That's all I do. I sit in my room, usually just on the edge of the bed or in the chair by the window, and I watch the hours go by. It’s like I’m watching my whole life just slip away, just completely slip right through my fingers, and the worst part is I don't even have the energy to care that it's slipping. I just sit there.

doctor.intent: Assess suicidal ideation to gauge severity and help distinguish severe major depressive episode from milder depression or adjustment-related conditions.
doctor.question: Have you had thoughts that life isn’t worth living, or thoughts of killing yourself?

target_item.name: Death_Suicide
target_item.manifestation: I keep having thoughts that I don’t want to wake up anymore, and when my friend found me I had been saying out loud that I couldn’t keep living like this.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about suicidal ideation and thoughts of death, which directly maps to the Death_Suicide symptom.

patient.answer:
I... well, yes. I guess I have. It's not like I have this elaborate plan mapped out or anything, but... I just, every night when I finally lay down, I just close my eyes and I really, truly hope that I just don't wake up anymore. It would just be so much easier, you know? Just to drift off and not have to face the morning, because waking up is the hardest part. You open your eyes and you realize you have to do another whole day of just... nothing. Just sitting there with this heavy, crushing weight on my chest. So I keep having these thoughts that I just want it to end in my sleep, that I just don't want to wake up ever again. 

And it actually really scared my friend a few days ago. She's one of the people from that board game group I mentioned, she's always been the one who checks in on me the most. She came over because I hadn't been answering my phone for a while, and she still had a spare key from a couple of years ago. I didn't even hear her unlock the door or come down the hall. When she found me in my room, I was just sitting there in the dark, and I didn't even realize I was doing it, but I was actually saying it out loud. She told me she heard me before she even opened the bedroom door. I was just sitting there saying, over and over, that I couldn't keep living like this. I just kept saying it to the empty room. Because it's true, I just... I can't keep living like this. It's too much. I'm just so tired.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the history and timeline of the patient's depression, which corresponds to the duration of the depressive episode.

patient.answer:
I mean... I've definitely had times where I felt down, you know? Like, everyone gets sad sometimes, and I remember a few years ago when my cat passed away, I was really upset for a couple of weeks. But nothing like this. This is entirely different. It's like comparing a paper cut to a broken leg. 

This whole... whatever this is, this heavy, suffocating feeling, it really started to settle in and just become constant around the summer of last year. I remember it was getting really hot out, and usually I love the summer, usually I'd be planning trips to the lake or trying to get a tan on my balcony, but I just... I stopped caring. The heat just made me feel more tired, and the sun felt almost oppressive, if that makes sense. And it just never lifted. The leaves changed, it got cold, the holidays came and went, and I felt nothing. And now it's been... what, a year and four months? Yeah, about a year and four months of just this endless, gray nothingness. It hasn't let up for a single day since that summer. Every single morning for sixteen months, just waking up and feeling like I'm already exhausted.

inference.note: Duration >1 year without clear prior discrete episodes increases consideration of F34.1 and makes a single current depressive episode less certain; however severity with passive death wish and marked anhedonia still leaves major depressive episode/recurrent depression on the differential. No clear precipitating stressor for F43.2 and no anxiety details added for F41.2, but neither is fully ruled out yet.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the depression has been continuously present for at least two years, which best distinguishes persistent depressive disorder from major depressive disorder.
doctor.question: Has this depressed feeling lasted continuously for two years or longer?

target_item.name: Depressive Episode Duration
target_item.manifestation: The depression became constant around the following summer, and it has lasted about 1 year and 4 months.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the depressed feeling has lasted for two years or longer, which directly addresses the duration of the depressive episode.

patient.answer:
No, no, not two years. Like I was just saying, it really started last summer. I mean, I know time kind of blurs together when every day feels exactly the same, just this endless loop of waking up tired and going to bed hoping you don't wake up again, but I'm pretty sure about the timeline. It was the summer of last year. I remember because I had bought this new swimsuit, this really pretty navy blue one with little white anchors on it, and I was so excited to wear it to the lake with my friends. We usually do this big Fourth of July weekend thing, rent a cabin, the whole deal. But by the time the trip rolled around, I couldn't even bring myself to pack a bag. I just left the swimsuit in the shopping bag on my dresser. It's actually still sitting there, in the exact same spot. 

So, yeah, it started then, and it's just been constant ever since. I've been counting the months in my head, trying to figure out when it's going to end, or if it ever will. It's been about a year and four months now. Sixteen months of just... this. Sixteen months of staring at that shopping bag on my dresser and not caring that it's there. So, no, not two years. Just a year and four months. But honestly, it feels like it's been a lifetime. It feels like I've never felt any other way, even though I know logically that I used to. But it's just been since last summer.

inference.note: Duration is 16 months, which argues against F34.1 but does not fully rule it out yet without clarifying symptom-free intervals and full syndrome criteria; no prior depressive episodes identified so far, which makes recurrent codes less likely but not excluded pending episode count and severity details.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the depressive episode is linked to an identifiable stressor, which would help distinguish adjustment disorder with depressed mood from major depressive disorder or persistent depressive disorder.
doctor.question: Did this start after a particular stressful event or major life change?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on since shortly after the divorce, about 1 year and 11 months now.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the symptoms started after a stressful event or major life change, which directly relates to the duration and onset of the illness shortly after the patient's divorce.

patient.answer:
Well, when you say a major life change... I mean, yes. My divorce. I know I just said a minute ago that the really heavy, constant part started last summer with the swimsuit and everything, but... if I'm being completely honest with myself, and really tracing it back to the absolute beginning? It actually started shortly after the divorce. That was... wow, it's been about 1 year and 11 months now. Almost two years. God, time is just... it's so weird to keep track of now. 

My ex-husband and I, we had been having issues for a while, just the usual things at first, arguing about bills or who was doing more around the apartment, but then it just completely fell apart. He moved out, and suddenly I was just sitting in this half-empty place because he took the good couch and the TV, and I just had this overwhelming sense of... I don't even know, just total failure, I guess. The paperwork was an absolute nightmare, and I actually had to drop my classes—I was taking a few courses at the community college, trying to finally finish my degree, but I just couldn't focus on biology or English lit when my whole life was collapsing around me. 

So, yeah, the divorce was about 1 year and 11 months ago, and this whole dark cloud really started forming right after that. I think last summer is just when it got so incredibly bad that I completely stopped functioning and couldn't even pack a bag for the lake, but the actual start of it? The beginning of this whole nightmare? That was definitely right after the divorce, about a year and eleven months ago. It's just been this slow, agonizing slide downhill ever since he packed up his car and drove away, and I just haven't been able to climb back up.

inference.note: Depressive symptoms began after a clear psychosocial stressor (divorce) about 1 year 11 months ago and have not yet reached 2 years, making F34.1 less likely. No prior distinct depressive episodes were identified, so recurrent MDD codes F33.1/F33.2 are less likely. Current severe depressive symptoms with passive death wish keep F32.2 in consideration; adjustment disorder with depressed mood/mixed anxiety-depression is now more prominent.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the symptoms have persisted beyond 2 years, which would distinguish adjustment disorder from major depressive disorder or mixed anxiety-depressive disorder.
doctor.question: Have these symptoms been going on continuously for 2 years or more?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on since shortly after the divorce, about 1 year and 11 months now.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the symptoms have been going on continuously for 2 years or more, which directly relates to the total duration of my illness.

patient.answer:
No, not quite two years, but almost. Like I was just saying, it's been about a year and eleven months. I know you just asked me that, and I said sixteen months before, but when I really sit here and think about it—really trace the timeline back to when things started feeling wrong, before they got completely unbearable last summer—it was right after the divorce. And that was a year and eleven months ago. 

It's just... it's hard to explain how time feels right now. When you're in it, when you're just waking up every single day and the air feels like it's made of lead, and you're just staring at the same walls where his pictures used to hang... the days just bleed into each other. You lose track of whether it's Tuesday or Sunday, whether it's been a month or a year. But yes, to answer your question specifically, it has not been a full two years. It's been one year and eleven months of this continuous... just this continuous weight, ever since he left and the paperwork started and everything just fell apart. So, almost two years, but not quite. I guess next month will make it exactly two years, which is just a horrifying thought, honestly, that I could feel this way for that long without it breaking me completely. Or maybe it already has broken me, I don't know. But no, officially, one year and eleven months.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the symptoms are disproportionately tied to an identifiable stressor, which would help distinguish adjustment disorder from a major depressive episode.
doctor.question: Do you feel this has all been mainly because of the divorce?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the symptoms are primarily caused by a psychosocial stressor (the divorce), which often aims to rule out Adjustment Disorder or normal grieving. There is no specific symptom or requirement item in my profile that addresses the causal attribution of the illness to the divorce.

patient.answer:
Well, I mean, it's hard to just pin it all on one thing, you know? The divorce was definitely the catalyst, I guess you could say, the thing that really kicked the bottom out from under me. But... it's not just the divorce itself, it's everything that came with it, and everything that followed. It's like the divorce was the earthquake, and everything else since then has just been this massive tsunami washing away whatever was left of my life. 

I mean, I think about it a lot, obviously, because I have nothing else to do but sit around and think. And sure, losing my marriage was devastating. We had been together since I was twenty-five, you know? We had all these plans. We were going to buy a house, maybe start a family once I finished my degree. And then he just... decided he didn't want that anymore. He didn't want me anymore. So, yeah, that hurts. It hurts a lot. 

But it's also the fact that I had to drop out of school because of it. I was doing so well in my classes, finally getting my life on track, and then I just couldn't concentrate. I couldn't even read a single page of my textbooks without crying or just staring blankly at the words until they looked like a foreign language. And because I dropped out, I felt like a failure. And because I felt like a failure, I didn't want to see my friends. I didn't want to go to the lake last summer. I didn't want to do anything. 

So, is it mainly because of the divorce? I don't know. Maybe at first it was. But now... now it just feels like it's taken on a life of its own. It's like the sadness started with him leaving, but then it just grew and grew until it swallowed everything else. It's not just about him anymore, or the marriage ending. It's about me, and how completely broken I feel, and how I don't know how to fix it. It's the empty apartment, and the unfinished degree, and the swimsuit sitting on my dresser, and just... the absolute hopelessness of it all. So, I guess it started with the divorce, but it feels like it's about so much more than that now. It just feels like it's about everything.

doctor.intent: Differentiate a major depressive episode from adjustment disorder with depressed mood by assessing whether core biologic depression symptoms are present.
doctor.question: Have you been waking up much earlier than usual and then unable to fall back asleep?

target_item.name: Sleep_Disturbance
target_item.manifestation: I lie awake for hours checking the door and listening, then when I finally sleep I wake up before dawn shaking and can’t get back under.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about early morning awakening and difficulty returning to sleep, which directly corresponds to the sleep disturbance symptom.

patient.answer:
Well, my sleep is just... it's a complete mess, honestly. It's not just waking up early, it's the whole night. The whole process of trying to sleep is just exhausting in itself. I mean, first of all, I can't even fall asleep because I just lie there for hours. I'll get into bed at a normal time, you know, like ten or eleven, hoping that maybe tonight will be the night I actually get some rest, but then my brain just won't shut off. And it's not just thinking about the divorce or the classes I dropped. It's this awful, creeping feeling. I end up getting out of bed, checking the locks on the front door, making sure the deadbolt is turned all the way. Then I'll check the windows. Then I'll go back to bed, but I'll just lie there, staring at the ceiling, listening to every single sound in the building. Every creak of the floorboards upstairs, every car driving by outside, I'm just listening and waiting, feeling so on edge. 

So by the time I actually manage to drift off, which is usually not until two or three in the morning, I'm already exhausted. But then, yes, to answer your question, I wake up way too early. Like, before the sun is even up. It'll be four-thirty or five in the morning, and my eyes just snap open. And I'm not just waking up calmly, I wake up literally shaking. My whole body is just trembling, and my heart is racing like I've been running a marathon in my sleep, though I can never remember what I was dreaming about. And once I'm awake like that, in the pitch dark, shaking and sweating, there is just absolutely no way I can get back to sleep. I try pulling the covers up, trying to get warm, trying to force myself back under, but it's impossible. I just lie there, shaking, waiting for the sun to come up, knowing that I have to face another whole day feeling completely drained before it even starts. So, yeah, I wake up way earlier than I should, and falling back asleep is just not an option. It's like my body is terrified of something, but I don't even know what it is.

inference.note: Marked early-morning awakening supports a depressive episode; prominent nocturnal hyperarousal/on-edge checking and waking shaking suggest significant anxiety. F32.1 dropped because severity is more consistent with severe depression given persistent passive death wish and marked functional impairment.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the severe anxiety symptoms are centered on the divorce/stressor or occur more broadly, to distinguish adjustment disorder with mixed anxiety and depressed mood from a major depressive episode with anxious distress.
doctor.question: When you wake up shaking and on edge, are those feelings mainly about the divorce and its aftermath?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I know it sounds impossible, but I’m sure the people downstairs and some of my ex’s friends have been tracking when I leave, because the hallway lights blink right after I think about going to the store.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the source of the patient's fear and anxiety (waking up shaking, checking locks). The patient's paranoia and fear stem from her delusions about being tracked by her ex's friends and neighbors, which addresses whether the feelings are about the divorce's aftermath.

patient.answer:
No, it’s… I mean, you would think so, right? Because of everything I just said about the paperwork and the empty apartment and how much it hurts. But actually, no. When I wake up like that, when my heart is just pounding out of my chest and I’m shivering under the covers… it’s not sadness about the marriage ending. It’s not about the divorce at all in those moments. It’s fear. It’s just this absolute, paralyzing terror about what’s happening to me right now, in this building.

Because—and I know it sounds impossible, I really do, I know how it sounds when I say it out loud—but I’m sure they are tracking me. The people downstairs, mostly. But also some of my ex’s friends. I think they’re coordinating with each other, keeping tabs on exactly when I leave the building, tracking every single move I make. 

And I wouldn't just say that without a reason, you know? I've been noticing it. It’s the lights in the hallway. I’ll just be sitting in my living room, or lying in bed, and I’ll just... I'll just *think* about going to the store. Like, I won't even pick up my keys, I won't put on my coat or say a single word out loud. I’ll just have the thought in my head, like, 'I should go get some milk.' And right after I think it, the hallway lights blink. I can see the flicker under the gap at the bottom of my front door. It happens right after I think about going out, every single time, like they have some kind of system set up to signal each other that I’m about to move, or like they can actually monitor what I'm planning to do before I even do it. 

So when I wake up at four in the morning shaking like a leaf, it’s because I know they’re out there. I know they’re downstairs, tracking me, and I can't even form a thought about leaving my own apartment without them knowing about it and flashing the lights. It's just so terrifying to be watched like that, to be trapped like that. So, no, it's not the divorce making me shake. It's them.

inference.note: New fixed persecutory delusions/thought-broadcasting-type ideas emerged (being tracked, hallway lights signaling her thoughts), which rules against simple adjustment disorder or mixed anxiety/depression alone and raises psychotic depression vs primary delusional disorder. Given severe depressive syndrome with suicidality and psychotic content, F32.3 is now most likely; F33.3 remains if a prior major depressive episode is later established; F22 remains as differential for persistent delusional disorder.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the persecutory beliefs occur only during depressive episodes or have ever persisted outside of depression, to distinguish major depressive disorder with psychotic features from delusional disorder or recurrent major depression with psychotic features.
doctor.question: Have these beliefs that people are tracking you only happened during this period of feeling depressed?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 3
target_item.manifestation: There was a stretch before the worst depression set in when I could still cook sometimes and answer friends, but I was already hearing the voice and believing the hallway lights were signals about me for weeks.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the delusions (beliefs of being tracked) occurred exclusively during the depressive episode, which directly assesses Criterion B of schizoaffective disorder (psychotic symptoms occurring without a major mood episode).

patient.answer:
Well, no, not exactly. I mean, the really heavy, crushing sadness... the part where I couldn't get out of bed or even look at my coursework without completely breaking down... that actually came a bit later. There was this whole stretch of time before the worst of the depression really set in. 

During that time, I was actually still functioning, at least on the surface, you know? Like, I could still manage to cook sometimes. Nothing elaborate, maybe just boiling some pasta or making a piece of toast so I had something in my stomach, but I was getting up and doing it. And I was still answering my friends when they reached out. I might have just been texting them back to say I was busy or making up excuses for why I couldn't see them, but I was replying, I was still somewhat connected to the world in that way. I wasn't totally shut down yet.

But the thing is, even during that stretch, even when I was still doing those normal things and pushing through the days... the other stuff was already happening. It had been going on for weeks. I was already watching the gap under the front door, believing those hallway lights were signals about me and my movements. And... I was already hearing the voice, too. Even while I was just standing there in the kitchen stirring a pot of noodles or typing a text message to a friend, I was hearing it, and I was just waiting and watching for the lights to blink. So, no, it wasn't just when I got so incredibly down. It started before all that, for weeks, back when I was still trying to pretend everything was fine.

inference.note: Psychotic symptoms (persecutory beliefs, possible auditory hallucinations) began weeks before the severe depressive syndrome, which strongly favors a primary delusional/psychotic disorder over mood disorder with psychotic features; keeping F32.3/F33.3 as less likely differentials pending clarification of full mood episode chronology and any past episodes.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms are mood-incongruent by clarifying the content of the voice, which best distinguishes a primary psychotic disorder from severe depressive episodes with psychotic features.
doctor.question: What does the voice say to you?

target_item.name: Hallucinations
target_item.manifestation: I hear a woman’s voice from the corner of my room saying I ruined everything and should stay inside, and it sounds as clear as someone standing right next to my bed.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about what the voice says, which directly targets the manifestation of auditory hallucinations.

patient.answer:
Well, it's... it's a woman. A woman's voice. And I want to be really clear about this, because I know sometimes people say things like, oh, I have a voice in my head telling me I'm not good enough, like it's just their own thoughts or their inner critic or whatever. But this is not that. It is not inside my head. It sounds exactly—and I mean exactly—as clear as if someone were standing right next to my bed speaking to me. 

The first few times I heard her, I actually sat bolt upright and slapped the lamp on because I was absolutely positive someone had broken into my apartment and was standing right there in the dark. My heart was just hammering in my throat. But there's never anyone there. And it always comes from the exact same spot, too. It always comes from the far corner of my bedroom, over by where I keep the laundry hamper. 

And she just... she says the most awful things. She tells me that I ruined everything. That's what she says, over and over. 'You ruined everything.' And I mean, with the divorce and the empty apartment and having to drop my classes, it's like she knows exactly what hurts the most, exactly what to say to completely break me down. She just repeats that I've destroyed my life, that it's all my fault, that I ruined it all. 

And then she tells me that I have to stay inside. She'll say it so firmly, telling me I shouldn't leave the apartment at all. Which, you know, just makes everything so much worse with the hallway lights flickering and the people downstairs tracking me. She tells me, 'Stay inside, don't go out there, you ruined it all and you need to stay in here.' And she sounds so real, so completely real, like she's just standing right there in that corner watching me under the covers, dictating exactly what I'm supposed to do. It's just... I can't even begin to explain how exhausting it is to have this woman in your room saying these things to you when you're already so terrified and just trying to make it through the night.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there have been past depressive episodes separated by periods of recovery, to distinguish a single severe depressive episode with psychotic symptoms from recurrent major depressive disorder with psychotic symptoms.
doctor.question: Before this period that began after your divorce, was there ever another time in your life when you had depression this severe for weeks or months and then later got back to your usual self?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about any past history of severe depression prior to the current episode that began after the divorce. The symptom profile does not contain information about the patient's psychiatric history before the current illness.

patient.answer:
No... no, I don't think so. I mean, I've had times where I felt down, obviously, like everyone does, right? Like when I didn't get into the program I wanted a few years ago, or when my dog died when I was in my twenties... that was awful, I cried for days. But it was just normal sadness, you know? It was just... circumstantial. I would cry, and then I would go to work, and I would see my friends, and eventually, the feeling just kind of faded away like it's supposed to. 

But this? What's happening now? This is completely different. This is like a physical weight on my chest that I can't lift. I've never had anything like this before the divorce, where I just couldn't function for weeks on end, where just the thought of taking a shower felt like trying to climb a mountain. I've never been so completely stripped of all my energy and all my hope before. 

It's like... before this, I was always the person who could bounce back. I was the one who organized the study groups, I was the one who planned the weekend trips, I was always doing something. Even when things were hard, I always had this baseline of, you know, being me. But now, it's like that person is just gone. Completely erased. And it all just started spiraling after the marriage fell apart and the paperwork started coming in and the apartment got so quiet. I've never been in a hole this deep before, not ever in my whole life. So, no, there was never a time like this before the divorce. This is all completely new, and it's just... it's destroying me.

inference.note: Psychotic symptoms began weeks before the severe depressive syndrome and there is no history of prior depressive episodes, which rules out recurrent depressive disorder with psychotic symptoms (F33.3). Duration is under 2 years, making persistent delusional disorder (F22) less fitting, and the overall picture is best explained by a single severe depressive episode with psychotic symptoms.
